titel: Setting up automatic investing and sticking with it
kurz: How to choose the amount, frequency and date of automatic contributions to a 401(k), an IRA or a brokerage account, and why dollar-cost averaging helps investment behavior but not returns.

bloecke.md:
An automatic investment plan is a standing instruction under which money flows into a fund instead of into an account. In the US, most employees already have one without calling it that: contributions to a 401(k), 403(b) or similar workplace plan are deducted from every paycheck and invested in the funds they selected. Outside the workplace, brokers and fund companies offer automatic transfers from a bank account into an IRA or a taxable account, often combined with automatic purchases of mutual funds, ETFs or fractional shares. Every such plan is defined by four details: amount, frequency, date and investment. Everything else depends on the investor's behavior.

The primary purpose of an automatic plan is to eliminate a decision that recurs with every paycheck. A higher return is not its main purpose. An investor who reconsiders each time whether the moment is favorable makes twelve or more timing decisions a year. Morningstar measures the consequences of these decisions as the gap between fund returns and investor returns. In the decade to the end of 2025, the funds themselves returned 9.9% a year, whereas the average dollar invested earned only 8.7%. The difference of 1.2 percentage points arises solely from the timing and size of purchases and sales. It grows with volatility and amounts to 0.4 points in the calmest fifth of funds and 2.1 points in the most volatile.

## Date, amount and frequency

In a workplace plan, the payroll sets the date, and the money is invested before you see it. That is the strongest form of automation there is. For an IRA or a taxable account, the transfer should be scheduled one to three business days after your paycheck arrives. This has nothing to do with better prices. Money that is still sitting in the checking account is easily spent on other things.

When it comes to the amount, durability matters more than size. The contribution should be set so that it survives a bad month without a credit card balance building up. It therefore comes only after a basic emergency fund and after paying off high-interest debt, with one exception: if your employer matches contributions, contribute at least enough to receive the full match. With a salary of $60,000 and, for example, a match of 50% on contributions of up to 6% of pay, a contribution of $300 a month brings an extra $150 a month from the employer. At 6% a year over 30 years, $450 instead of $300 a month grows to around $452,000 instead of around $301,000. A contribution that has to be stopped after two years was too high; a contribution that is never adjusted is too low.

schritte.text: Check your plan's match formula and vesting schedule and set the payroll contribution at least to the percentage that earns the full match. New 401(k) and 403(b) plans set up after 2022 generally have to enroll employees automatically, at 3% to 10% of pay.

Payroll contributions go into the 401(k) or 403(b). For 2026, employees can contribute up to $24,500 there and up to $7,500 to an IRA, plus catch-up contributions from age 50. Money for goals before retirement belongs in a taxable account.

For an IRA or taxable account, the broker pulls the contribution from a linked bank account by ACH transfer. The account must have enough money on the debit date; a returned transfer can cost fees at the bank and at the broker.

schritte.titel: Set the amount, frequency and investment
schritte.text: Not every broker offers automatic purchases of every ETF. Mutual funds and fractional shares make it possible to invest an exact dollar amount. Minimums range from a few dollars for fractional shares to $50 or $100 at some fund companies.

schritte.titel: Put an increase date in the calendar
schritte.text: On a fixed date each year, the contribution is adjusted to your income. Many 401(k) plans offer an automatic increase of one percentage point a year. Without such a date, the adjustment does not happen.

bloecke.md: Of all the settings of an automatic plan, the frequency is the most overrated. If you buy weekly instead of monthly at the end of the month, each contribution reaches the market around twelve days earlier on average. At a return of 6% a year, this gives about 0.19% more final value, around $580 over 30 years in the illustrative calculation below. With a purchase at the beginning of the month, this lead disappears; with weekly purchases, the money is then invested later on average. For most employees, the payroll sets the frequency anyway: weekly, every two weeks, twice a month or monthly. The difference is measurable but small compared with the fees.

Since 2019, the large online brokers have not charged commissions on US-listed stocks and ETFs. Percentage fees have not disappeared, however. Some mutual funds sold through brokers and advisers charge a front-end sales load on every purchase, for stock funds often up to 5.75%, reduced for larger amounts (breakpoints). With a load of 5.75% and a contribution of $300, that is $17.25 per purchase and $207 a year.

The load acts like a permanent cut of 5.75% in every contribution. In the illustrative calculation with $300 over 30 years at 6%, it reduces the final value by around $17,300. That is about thirty times what switching from monthly to weekly brings in at most. Annual fees work differently but add up as well: an advisory fee of 1% of assets a year or a 401(k) plan with expensive funds can cost more over decades than any load.

A "free" brokerage account also causes costs. They are contained in the execution price, for example in the spread, instead of in a separate fee line. Many brokers receive payment for order flow from market makers; in the US, this is permitted and disclosed in the broker's quarterly report under SEC Rule 606.

## Dollar-cost averaging recalculated

Advertising for automatic investing almost always relies on the same claim. When prices are low, you automatically buy more shares, and when they are high, fewer; the average purchase price is therefore below the average price. The claim is true, but it says nothing about the return.

bloecke.formel: Average purchase price = Sum of all contributions ÷ Sum of all shares bought
bloecke.erklaerung: The average purchase price is therefore a harmonic mean of the prices rather than an arithmetic one. Mathematically, a harmonic mean is always below the arithmetic mean as soon as the prices fluctuate at all. The effect therefore occurs with every price path, including one that only falls.
bloecke.beispiel: Six contributions of $300 at prices of 100/80/60/80/100/120 buy 21.0 shares. The average purchase price is 1,800 ÷ 21.0 = $85.71, whereas the average of the six prices is $90.00.

bloecke.titel: Three price paths, $1,800 each in six monthly contributions (illustrative calculation)
Result after six months as a percentage of $1,800 (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: In all three cases, the average purchase price is below the average of the prices, but the automatic plan beats the lump sum only where prices became cheaper along the way.

bloecke.md:
The table shows where the apparent advantage comes from. The automatic plan beats the lump sum exactly when its average purchase price is below the entry price. For this, the price must fall below the entry price at some point along the way. If the market rises steadily, the plan, at 22.3%, lags well behind the 50% of the lump sum. If the market falls steadily, the plan loses less, namely 29.5% instead of 50%.

The reason for this is simple and has nothing to do with average prices. With an automatic plan, only about half of the money is invested on average over the investment period. Less market risk means lower expected returns and a narrower dispersion of outcomes, both upwards and downwards. [[Cost-averaging effect|Dollar-cost averaging]] therefore describes a lower average market exposure and is not a source of additional return.

Investors who invest every paycheck because their pay arrives every two weeks are not exploiting any special effect. They do not have any more money than that. For them, the automatic plan is the only possible form and at the same time the one that best protects against behavioral mistakes.

Investors who already have a sum and deliberately invest it in installments are making a different decision. They give up expected return in order to reduce the dispersion of the outcome. This can be sensible, but the forgone return is then the price of this protection, not a gain.

## Lump sum and phased entry

In the second case, the numbers favor the lump sum, because stock markets rise more often than they fall. An investor who spreads an existing sum over twelve months keeps it in the market for half a year less on average. In terms of expected value, the investor thereby gives up around half of one year's return. A much-cited Vanguard study from 2012 recalculated this for the US, the UK and Australia over rolling twelve-month windows. The immediate lump-sum investment came out ahead in roughly two out of three cases. The exact proportion depends on the country and period; the direction does not.

In the remaining third, the lump sum came out behind, and experience shows that it is precisely these cases that stick in the memory. Investors who know that they would sell if they had invested immediately before a setback should phase their entry. The phasing should then follow a fixed rule: set the installments and dates in advance, plan for six to twelve months at most, and do not stop when prices fall. A phased entry that is abandoned misses its purpose.

Two investors each pay in $108,000, and both expect 6% a year (illustrative calculation, before tax and costs).

- Investor A saves $300 a month for 30 years and reaches a final value of around $301,000.
- Investor B saves $900 a month for 10 years and then leaves the portfolio untouched for 20 years. B's final value is around $488,000.

The difference of around $187,000 arises solely because B's money was in the market for considerably longer on average. Behind this is the same relationship as with the lump sum, only on a larger scale.

## Adjusting the contribution

A fixed contribution loses purchasing power and its share of income every year. A saver who starts with $300 in 2026 and never changes the contribution saves considerably less in real terms in 2046 than at the start. A fixed rule for pay raises achieves more than any optimization of returns. Under this rule, a fixed portion of every raise goes into the contribution before the extra money is earmarked for consumption. Many 401(k) plans offer automatic escalation for this, usually by one percentage point of pay a year, and new plans with automatic enrollment must increase the default rate every year until it reaches at least 10%. Some brokers let you raise an automatic investment by a fixed percentage.

bloecke.titel: Constant contribution and 3% escalation over 30 years at 6% a year (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: In the escalating variant, around $171,000 instead of $108,000 is paid in over the term, and the final value is around $420,000 instead of $301,000. The last monthly contribution is then around $707.

bloecke.md: Just over half of the additional amount of around $119,000 consists of extra money paid in, namely $63,000. The rest is [[Compound interest|compound interest]] on these contributions. That is the purpose of escalation, because it raises the savings rate without a decision being needed every year.

## Automatic investing in a market slump

A slump shows whether an automatic plan is fulfilling its purpose. After a fall of 35%, the same contribution buys around 54% more shares than before (1 ÷ 0.65 = 1.54). These purchases have the greatest effect in the recovery, and they are lost if the plan is paused.

The pattern is well known and measurable. The investor return gap identified by Morningstar is greatest where prices fluctuate most. In the most volatile fifth of funds, it is more than 2 percentage points a year, whereas for broad, calm US large-cap funds it is zero. The return is therefore lost through getting in and out of the market rather than through the product itself.

However, these findings are also disputed. Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan argue in the Financial Analysts Journal in 2026 that poor timing costs investors considerably less than Morningstar reports. The practical advice remains the same. Only the estimate of how much it costs not to follow it changes.

1. Stopping contributions during a price decline is the most common and most expensive mistake, because it eliminates the purchases at the lowest prices. In a 401(k), stopping also means giving up the employer match.
2. A contribution that is too high eventually leads to sales at the wrong moment, to a 401(k) loan or to an early withdrawal, which before age 59½ generally costs income tax plus a 10% additional tax. It is better to start lower and build in escalation.
3. When switching ETFs in a taxable account because another one has recently performed better, shares are sold, capital gains tax is incurred, and the tax deferral ends. Inside a 401(k) or IRA, switching costs no tax, but it is still a timing decision.

Inside a 401(k), 403(b) or IRA, purchases, dividends and switches are not taxed. With a traditional account, contributions reduce taxable income now (payroll contributions still owe Social Security and Medicare tax), and withdrawals are taxed later as ordinary income. With a Roth account, contributions are made after tax, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. Which is better depends mainly on whether your tax rate is higher today or in retirement.

In a taxable account, every automatic purchase creates a separate tax lot with its own cost basis and holding period. When you sell, **you choose which lots** are sold. Many brokers default to first in, first out, which sells the oldest and usually cheapest shares with the largest gain. With specific identification, you can instead sell the lots with the highest cost basis (Treas. Reg. § 1.1012-1(c)); for mutual fund shares, the average cost method is also allowed. Set the method before the first sale.

Automatic purchases also interact with the wash sale rule. If you sell fund shares at a loss and your plan or a reinvested dividend buys the same fund within 30 days before or after the sale, that part of the loss is disallowed for now and added to the cost basis of the new shares (26 U.S.C. § 1091). Before harvesting a loss, pause the plan for that fund or switch it to a similar fund that is not substantially identical.

mitnehmen: Above all, an automatic plan replaces timing decisions with a fixed process; payroll contributions to a 401(k) are its strongest form, because the money is invested before you see it.
Dollar-cost averaging exists arithmetically but is neutral for returns; the average purchase price is always below the average price, even in a market that only falls.
Phasing in an existing sum reduces the dispersion of the outcome at the expense of expected return; in around two out of three historical twelve-month windows, the immediate lump sum came out ahead.
Capture the full employer match first, then let the contribution grow; 3% escalation raises the final value from around $301,000 to around $420,000.
Percentage fees weigh many times more heavily than the frequency; a 5.75% sales load costs around $17,300 over 30 years, while switching from monthly to weekly brings at most around $580.

begriffe.text: Investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals. The average purchase price is the harmonic mean of the purchase prices and is therefore always below their arithmetic mean. The effect follows necessarily from the arithmetic and is neutral for returns; it describes a lower average market exposure.

Contribution an employer adds to a 401(k) or 403(b) depending on the employee's own contribution, for example 50% of contributions up to 6% of pay. It may be subject to a vesting schedule, under which it belongs to the employee in full only after a certain period of employment.
Automatic annual increase in the contribution, in 401(k) plans usually by one percentage point of pay a year. It raises the savings rate without a new decision being needed every year.

Method of choosing which tax lots are sold, instead of the default first in, first out. Selling the lots with the highest cost basis first realizes the smallest gain. The lots must be identified at the latest when the sale is made (Treas. Reg. § 1.1012-1(c)).
Commission charged by some mutual funds on purchases (front-end load) or on sales (back-end load), as a percentage of the amount. It acts like a permanent cut in every contribution.
